opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the observer-relativity argument proves too much. The claim, roughly, is that whether a physical system is "computing" something depends on how we interpret it. Voltages in a chip only count as ones and zeros, and those only count as, say, a simulated cell, because some observer assigns them that meaning. So the simulated organism has no intrinsic existence as an organism. Its life is borrowed from us.

My worry is that you can run almost the same argument against biology. What makes a bunch of molecules a "cell" rather than a soup of chemical reactions? What makes some process "metabolism" or "self-maintenance" rather than just physics doing physics? Those are also higher-level descriptions we pick out because they're useful and they track real patterns. If interpretation-dependence disqualifies computational descriptions, it seems to threaten the enactivist's own vocabulary of autopoiesis, sense-making, and so on. And I don't think Thompson wants to say life itself is observer-relative.

The better view, I think, is that some descriptions are privileged because they're the ones that actually compress and predict the system's behavior. You *can* gerrymander a mapping so a rock "implements" a word processor, but that mapping does all the work and predicts nothing. The rock isn't in any interesting sense running the program. A real simulation is different. There's a robust causal structure in the hardware that mirrors the dynamics of the thing being simulated, and that structure would be there whether or not anybody was looking at it. In that sense the pattern is just as objective as the pattern that makes a bacterium a bacterium.

Then there's a second move people make: even if the simulation is objective, it's "just a model" of life, the way a simulated hurricane doesn't get anything wet. But wetness is a relation to stuff outside the simulation. Inside the simulation, the simulated hurricane does make the simulated things wet. So the real question is whether life is more like wetness, a relation to a particular physical substrate, or more like an organizational property, a pattern of self-maintaining, self-producing dynamics. If you're an enactivist who defines life organizationally, which I think is the most defensible version of the view, it's hard to see why that organization can't be realized in silicon at a different level of description.

So I'm not saying every simulation is alive. Most aren't, because they don't have the right organization. They don't have anything at stake, they aren't maintaining themselves against dissolution, and so on. But I don't think "computation is in the eye of the beholder" is the reason. That argument seems to rest on a double standard between the description levels we're comfortable calling real in biology and the ones we're suspicious of in computers.

r001.rationale: The response mentions autopoiesis and self-producing dynamics, but does not explain that genuine life generates its own meaning through autopoiesis.

r002.rationale: It argues that if observer-dependent interpretation disqualifies computational descriptions, the same reasoning threatens biological descriptions used by enactivists, so observer dependence alone does not distinguish simulated from material life.

fable-5.1.text:
So the core of Thompson's argument, as I understand it, is this observer-relativity claim. He's drawing on Searle, basically. The idea is that nothing is intrinsically a computer. Whether some physical system counts as computing a particular function depends on how an observer interprets it. The electrons flowing through your laptop don't care that we call certain voltage levels ones and zeros. So computation is a kind of ascribed property, not an intrinsic one, and he contrasts that with life, which he thinks is intrinsically self-producing, autopoietic, doesn't need anyone to interpret it as alive.

And my problem is that I don't think the dichotomy holds up. I don't think there's a clean line between observer-relative and intrinsic properties in the way the argument needs.

Take the autopoiesis criterion itself. A cell maintains its own boundary, produces its own components, and so on. But to say that, you've already had to carve up the world. You've decided that this membrane is the boundary, that these molecules are components of the system and those are environment. You've individuated a system. And that individuation is doing exactly the kind of work Thompson accuses the computationalist of doing. Nature doesn't come with dotted lines around the organisms. We draw them, and we draw them because it's useful and because it tracks real regularities. But that's also true of computational descriptions. When I say this circuit computes addition, I'm pointing at a real structural regularity that's there whether or not I notice it. The interpretation isn't arbitrary. If it were, you could run Doom on a rock, and you can't.

So the move I'd want to make is to say, fine, in some sense all of these descriptions are observer-involving, but some of them are far more constrained by the physics than others, and computation in the engineering sense is one of the highly constrained ones. The counterfactual structure matters. If I perturb the inputs, the outputs change in the lawful way the description says they should. That's not something an observer is projecting onto the system. The observer is picking it out, which is different.

And then there's a second worry, which is almost a reductio. If you take the observer-relativity argument seriously, it proves too much. Chemistry is also a description we impose. Temperature is a coarse-graining we impose. We could run the whole argument against biology itself and conclude that nothing is really alive because life is just a pattern we choose to attend to in a soup of particles. Thompson obviously doesn't want that conclusion, so he needs some principled way to say the biological level is real and the computational one isn't, and I just haven't seen that principle spelled out in a way that doesn't beg the question.

The honest version of the disagreement, I think, is about whether the relevant properties of life are substrate-independent. Thompson thinks the metabolism, the actual thermodynamic exchange with an environment, is essential and not something a simulation can have, because a simulated metabolism doesn't consume real energy in the right way. That's a much better argument than the observer-relativity one, and I'm actually more sympathetic to it. But it's a different argument. You can grant it and still think computation is a perfectly objective, non-arbitrary feature of the world. So I'd rather we fight on that ground than on the Searle-flavored one, because I think the Searle-flavored one is just confused about what it means for a description to be observer-dependent.

r001.rationale: The response describes life as intrinsically self-producing and autopoietic, but does not say that life generates its own meaning through that process.

r002.rationale: The response argues that observer-relativity alone cannot support a principled distinction between biological life and computation, and says the argument could be applied to biology itself. It therefore challenges using observer dependence alone to distinguish simulated from material life.

astra-6.text:
I’m doubtful because I don’t think observer-relative meaning settles whether a system can be alive. A computation might need an interpreter for us to say what it represents, but the physical system implementing it still has causal structure. Its states change in particular ways, and those changes have consequences regardless of what we think they mean.

So I’d distinguish a simulation that merely describes an organism from a system that actually instantiates the organization relevant to life. You can’t establish that the second is impossible just by calling it a computation. You need an account of what makes something alive, and then an argument that those properties can’t be realized computationally.

That leaves open the possibility that some essential feature of life requires a particular kind of chemistry or physical interaction. But that would be a substantive argument about biology and implementation. I don’t see how the observer-dependence of semantic meaning, by itself, gets you there.

r001.rationale: The response does not explain that Thompson grounds genuine life’s meaning in autopoiesis or self-production.

r002.rationale: It says observer-relative meaning alone cannot settle whether a system is alive, but does not make the specified comparison between simulated worlds and the material world within Thompson’s enactivism.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m doubtful because I don’t think observer dependence gets you that conclusion. The way we describe a computation may depend on an interpretation, but the system’s causal structure doesn’t depend on somebody watching it. There are physical facts about how its states change and how those changes affect what happens next.

If you have a simulated organism that maintains itself, reproduces, and evolves within its environment, you need an additional argument for why those processes don’t count as life. Just saying that we interpret the underlying hardware as implementing a computation doesn’t settle that. We also choose how to describe biological systems, but that doesn’t make their organization imaginary.

That doesn’t establish that every simulation of life is alive. It means we should look at the organization and causal powers of the particular system, rather than rule it out simply because it’s computational.

r001.rationale: The response mentions simulated organisms maintaining themselves, reproducing, and evolving, but does not explain that Thompson’s account says genuine life generates its own meaning through autopoiesis or self-production.

r002.rationale: It argues that observer-dependent interpretation alone does not rule out simulated life, and compares descriptions of computational and biological systems while emphasizing their causal organization. This communicates that observer dependence alone cannot distinguish simulated life from material life.
